title: Pit firing basics — outdoor
subtitle: Setting up and running a simple pit firing in a garden or outdoor space for burnished earthenware
excerpt: Pit firing is one of the oldest ceramic firing methods: clay placed in a pit or trench with combustible material and fired in the open air. It produces unpredictable black, grey, and warm orange surface markings from flame and smoke contact, not glaze. The pieces must be burnished before firing; pit-fired work is decorative, not functional (porous after firing). This tutorial covers the outdoor setup, loading, and firing for a small pit fire.
sourceNotes: Pit firing methodology synthesised from contemporary studio ceramics practice and traditional ceramic firing references. Pit firing is documented across multiple Indigenous and studio pottery traditions.

content.text: Pit firing requires an outdoor space where an open fire is permitted. Check local authority regulations before firing. The fire reaches 800 to 900 °C at peak: keep a bucket of water and a fire extinguisher within reach throughout. Do not fire in windy conditions that could spread embers. The firing produces smoke: ensure neighbours are aware and downwind spaces are clear. Pit-fired work is NOT food-safe: the clay remains porous and the surface is decorative only.

Pit firing produces its characteristic markings from direct contact of flame and smoke with the clay surface. Where smoke is reduced and carbon deposits on the surface, the clay turns grey-black. Where flames contact the clay, the surface burns orange-red. The patterns are determined by how the pieces are loaded in the pit and what combustible materials are placed in contact with them. Salt, seaweed, copper wire, and iron oxides applied to the piece before firing all produce additional colour effects.

Build or throw pieces in a clay body suitable for low-fire conditions: earthenware-red or a grogged stoneware. Wall thickness should be 6 to 8 mm even throughout. Avoid thin sections: they crack first under
the surface with the back of a spoon or a polished stone. The burnish creates the smooth surface that allows flame markings to show clearly. For maximum effect, apply a coat of
(red or white) at leather-hard and burnish over it once dry.
Allow pieces to become fully bone-dry before firing: at least 48 hours in a warm dry space. Damp clay in a pit fire cracks from steam pressure in the first phase of firing.
Setting up and running the pit fire
Dig or set up a shallow pit or a metal container 40 to 60 cm deep. A metal dustbin with the bottom removed, or a purpose-built steel pit, contains the fire more reliably than a soil pit.

Lay a base layer of dry wood shavings or sawdust 15 cm deep at the bottom of the pit. Place the ceramic pieces on the sawdust layer, not touching each other. Surround and cover each piece with more sawdust, wood shavings, or combustible materials: banana skins (for copper colour), salted seaweed, crumpled newspaper, dried leaves. The more varied the combustible materials around each piece, the more varied the markings.

Add a top layer of kindling and small logs. Do not add accelerant. Light the fire from several points around the top. In the first 30 minutes, the fire burns through the combustible layers surrounding the pieces, generating smoke and flame that contact the clay surface directly.

Allow the fire to burn without interference for 2 to 3 hours. Add more wood to the top if the fire dies down before the 2-hour mark. A pit fire typically reaches 800 to 900 °C at peak: hot enough to fire earthenware to a hard, stable state.

After burning, cover the pit loosely with a metal lid or sheet to slow cooling. Leave undisturbed for a minimum of 6 hours: ideally overnight. Do not remove pieces until they are cool enough to handle comfortably with bare hands.

Remove pieces from the ash carefully. Wipe ash from the surface and polish with a soft cloth. A light wax polish (clear shoe wax or beeswax) enhances the burnished surface and provides minimal water resistance. Pit-fired pieces are decorative: do not use for food or liquid storage.

rows.problem: Pieces cracked in the pit fire
rows.cause: Clay not fully bone-dry; or fire built up too quickly; or wall thickness uneven
rows.fix: Allow longer drying time (minimum 48 hours). Use even wall thickness throughout. Start the fire slowly with newspaper and kindling rather than full wood load immediately.

rows.problem: Surface markings very faint: mostly uniform orange-red
rows.cause: Too little combustible material in contact with the piece; pieces too far from the fire material
rows.fix: Pack more sawdust, leaves, and organic material tightly around each piece. The more surface contact with combustible material, the more varied the carbon marks.

rows.problem: Pieces still warm after 6 hours: impatient opening cracked them
rows.cause: Rapid air cooling when the pit was uncovered too early
rows.fix: Leave the pit sealed for at least 12 hours before removal. The slower the cooling, the less thermal shock risk.
